implementation_notes: Vapor models the pattern directly: SessionsMiddleware reads the vapor_session cookie, restores req.session from the configured SessionDriver and synchronises changes back before the response is returned, while the driver decides where the payload lives - app.sessions.use(.memory) is the zero-configuration default the documentation recommends for testing only, .fluent stores records in the application's database (a _fluent_sessions table) and shares them across instances, and .redis keeps them in Redis. The driver must be configured before the middleware is added, because Sessions is a value type snapshotted at that point; req.session.destroy() deletes the record and invalidates the cookie.
code_sketch:
app.sessions.use(.redis)                       // driver first: value type
app.middleware.use(app.sessions.middleware)    // then the middleware

app.get("set", ":value") { req -> HTTPStatus in
    req.session.data["name"] = req.parameters.get("value")
    return .ok
}
app.get("del") { req -> HTTPStatus in
    req.session.destroy()                      // delete the server-side record
    return .ok
}
pitfalls: The default in-memory driver loses every session on restart and is explicitly documented as a testing choice; production needs .fluent or .redis so records survive and are shared between instances.
Configuring the driver after adding SessionsMiddleware silently keeps the previous store, because the Sessions value was already captured.
For pure APIs Vapor recommends stateless token authentication instead of sessions, so applying this pattern to a token-oriented backend adds a store without adding value.
